places.name: College City, no college
places.text: About two miles east is College City, home to about 290 people and no college at all. The town began with a school, Pierce Christian College, paid for with money from the estate of Andrew Pierce. The college opened in 1875 and left town in 1896.
places.more: Pierce died around 1871, and the sale of his property paid for the school. The College City post office opened in 1873, two years before classes began. A newspaper story in January 1875 listed two general stores, a hotel, a livery stable, a saddle shop, two blacksmith shops, a bakery, a drug store, a milliner and Chinese wash houses. The college building measured just 30 by 40 feet. When the college left, the local high school district took over its buildings, and today College City is served by the Pierce Joint Unified School District.

places.name: Tacitus Arbuckle's town
places.text: Arbuckle was laid out in 1875 and named for Tacitus Arbuckle, on whose ranch it grew. To get a town going, he gave lots to anyone who would build on them, and he became its first postmaster. The first train pulled in on July 4, 1876, just two months after the depot was finished.
places.more: Tacitus Arbuckle had started ranching here in 1866, nearly ten years before the town. According to the county, the town's depot is now the only train depot left in Colusa County. Today the farmland around Arbuckle mixes field crops with orchards, mostly almonds, and several almond hullers work nearby. Farming has also left a mark underground. A state study of more than 300 sites across the Sacramento Valley found that this area had sunk more than any other, with the town dropping 2.14 feet between 2008 and 2017. As water was pumped out of the aquifers below, the soil collapsed upon itself.

places.name: Almond orchards
places.text: The long, straight rows of trees around here are mostly almond orchards. In 2024 almonds were Colusa County's most valuable crop, worth about 279 million dollars, from roughly 63,000 acres. Almond pollination season usually runs from about mid-February to mid-March, when growers bring in honey bees to pollinate the blossoms.
places.more: Growers aim for about two hives per acre, and beekeepers truck their bees in from all over the United States. About two-thirds of the nation's commercial honey bee hives converge on California for almond season. In 2024, Colusa County almond growers used about 126,000 hives. The county's own beekeepers produced about 50,000 queen bees that year. Even the almond hulls are sold, worth about 5 million dollars in 2024.
places.spot: Look for orchard trees lined up in long, straight rows.

places.name: Sutter Buttes, closest view
places.text: On clear days, the cluster of peaks rising from the valley to the east is the Sutter Buttes, centered about 17 miles away. The Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga was the first European to see them, in 1806. In 1817 Luis Antonio Argüello named them los tres picos, the three peaks, and in 1843 John Frémont called them the Three Buttes.
places.more: John Sutter claimed the Buttes as part of his Mexican land grant, but American courts ruled that his grant did not include them, so every land title there traces back to the federal government. In June 1846, Frémont's party stopped at the Buttes and, fearing an attack, struck first, killing many Native people in what is known as the Sutter Buttes massacre. During the Gold Rush the peaks were called the Marysville Buttes, and in 1920 the state tried and failed to buy them. From 1962 to 1965, a Titan missile base with three underground silos was active on their north side. In 2003 the state bought 1,785 acres there for a park, but it is still not open to the public.
places.spot: Look for the Sutter Buttes and try to count their bumpy peaks.

places.name: Patwin homeland
places.text: The western Sacramento Valley is the homeland of the Patwin, the southern branch of the Wintun peoples. Their language has two main dialects: River Patwin, spoken along the Sacramento River, and Hill Patwin, in the hills and plains to the west. Today Patwin people are citizens of three federally recognized tribes, including the Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation, headquartered in Williams.
places.more: The Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation has about 270 citizens and holds the Cortina Rancheria, a 640-acre reservation in the hills about 15 miles west of Arbuckle. The other two Patwin tribes are the Cachil DeHe Band of Wintun Indians of the Colusa Indian Community and the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation. The Gold Rush brought disaster. Settlers took over acorn groves and water sources, smallpox and measles swept through the villages, and many Patwin were forced into unpaid labor. By the late 1850s only a fraction of the people survived. As of 2021, one person was documented as a first-language Patwin speaker, and tribal members are working to bring the language back.

places.name: Granzella's in Williams
places.text: In Williams, Granzella's has served the public since 1976. The family business includes a restaurant, deli, bakery and sports lounge, and it sells hand-packed jars of olives. Guy Fieri featured it on the Food Network, including its muffuletta sandwich.
places.more: A muffuletta is a round Sicilian sesame bread, and a sandwich made on it, created by a Sicilian immigrant to the United States and popularized in New Orleans. Granzella's grilled Reuben also made it onto Guy Fieri's show. Across the parking lot, the family runs Granzella's Inn, a 42-room motel. Williams became a city in 1920, and about 5,500 people lived here at the 2020 census.

places.name: Colusa and Korusi
places.text: Highway 20 leads about 8 miles east to Colusa, the county seat, on the Sacramento River. Its name comes from Korusi, a Patwin village that stood on the west bank of the river, where the city is today. In the 1850 law that created the county, the name was spelled Colusi, and newspapers often wrote Coluse.
places.more: In 1850 Charles Semple bought Rancho Colus, a Mexican land grant first given to John Bidwell, and founded the town, first calling the spot Salmon Bend. The legislature settled on the spelling Colusa in 1854. Rest stops for travelers grew up at set road distances from town, from Five Mile House to Seventeen Mile House. Colusa still has a historic Chinatown, a Carnegie library from 1905, and a courthouse built in 1861 that is a California Historical Landmark. The river runs behind a levee so high that it is hard to see from town.

places.name: Rice country
places.text: Many of the flat fields around here are rice paddies. In 2024, Colusa County harvested rice from about 118,000 acres, roughly 185 square miles, for a crop of more than half a million tons. Rice was the county's most valuable crop in 2023, and second only to almonds in 2024.
places.more: Growers once burned the leftover straw after harvest, but since 1992 a state law has limited burning. Many now flood their fields in winter instead and let the straw break down. Around 300,000 acres of Sacramento Valley rice fields are flooded each winter, and the California Rice Commission says they feed and shelter about 7 million ducks and geese. More than 200 kinds of wildlife use them, including sandhill cranes. The birds stock up on more than half the calories they need for their 2,000-mile flight north in spring.
places.spot: Look for flat fields covered with shallow water, sometimes full of birds.

places.name: Sites Reservoir, a lake to come
places.text: In a valley in the hills west of Maxwell, a new lake is planned: Sites Reservoir. Instead of damming a river, it would be filled with water taken from the Sacramento River during high flows, carried by canals and pumped up into the valley. Full, it would hold up to 1.5 million acre-feet, enough to serve 7.5 million people for a year.
places.more: The reservoir was first proposed in the 1950s, and serious droughts since then, most recently from 2011 to 2017, have raised worries about water supplies. It would stretch 13 miles north to south and 4 miles across, about 260 feet deep at its lowest point, making it the eighth largest reservoir in California. Two main dams, Sites Dam and Golden Gate Dam, plus nine small saddle dams would close the low spots in the hills. Water would arrive through the Tehama-Colusa Canal from a pumping plant at Red Bluff, and through another canal from Hamilton City. Construction is planned to begin in 2027, with operations by 2034. Diversions could at times take 60 percent of the river's flow, which could harm salmon and other fish.

places.name: Delevan refuge
places.text: About 5 miles east of the freeway lies Delevan National Wildlife Refuge, nearly 5,800 acres of managed marsh and upland. Each winter more than 200,000 ducks and 100,000 geese come to the refuge. Visitors can watch wildlife from a simple roadside overlook on the Maxwell-Colusa Highway.
places.more: The refuge holds more than 4,500 acres of intensively managed wetlands. Over the last 100 years about 95 percent of the Central Valley's wetlands have been lost, so waterfowl depend more and more on refuges like this one. Delevan also shelters rare species, including the giant garter snake, breeding tricolored blackbirds, and a large colony of an endangered plant called palmate-bracted bird's beak. Peregrine falcons and bald eagles spend the winter, and beavers, muskrats and black-tailed deer live there year round. Each year about 1,000 people stop at the overlook, and about 7,000 come to hunt.

places.name: Swift's Stone Corral
places.text: About 6 miles west of Maxwell stands Swift's Stone Corral, a state historical landmark since 1936. In 1850, rancher Granville Swift and his partner Frank Sears needed a corral, but there was no timber anywhere around, so they built one out of the flat stones scattered over the land.
places.more: Swift, a Kentuckian whose great-uncle was Daniel Boone, came to California at 19. In 1846 he was one of the 33 Americans who captured Sonoma in the Bear Flag Revolt, and he helped design the Bear Flag. After gold was discovered, he struck it rich at Bidwell's Bar, and with his brother and cousin he later bought 15,000 acres of Rancho Petaluma, near Sears Point. Swift buried an estimated 100,000 dollars in gold, and his handwritten list of hiding places survives, with notes like one tin box and one little bottle, both in the same hole. He later could not find many of them, and gold believed to be his has turned up several times since.

places.name: Tule fog
places.text: In winter this valley is known for tule fog, a thick ground fog named for the tule marshes of the Central Valley. It can stretch more than 400 miles, from Bakersfield all the way to Red Bluff. In the northern valley it usually clears sooner than in the south, because winter storms with strong winds and turbulent air pass through more often.
places.more: The official tule fog season runs from November 1 to March 31. The fog often brings drizzle, and when temperatures stay below freezing, that drizzle can leave an invisible glaze of black ice on the road. Its ups and downs have followed air pollution. Tule fog increased by 85 percent between 1930 and 1970, as farming and industry grew, then fell by 76 percent between 1980 and 2016, after air pollution rules took effect. Nitrogen oxides in the air react with ammonia to form tiny particles that help fog droplets condense, so as those emissions fell, so did the fog. In a fog bank on Interstate 5 near Elk Grove, south of Sacramento, 25 cars and nine big rigs collided on December 12, 1997.

places.name: Rancho Larkin's Children
places.text: East of here, along the river around Princeton, lay a land grant made out to children. Thomas Larkin, the United States consul in Monterey, would not become a Mexican citizen, so he could not get land himself. In 1844 he had three of his children naturalized, and two days later the children received a grant of about 44,000 acres.
places.more: Governor Manuel Micheltorena, who approved the grant, was heavily in debt to Larkin. Larkin sent a Missourian named John S. Williams to run the rancho, and in 1847 Williams built an adobe near an abandoned Patwin village called Chah'de'-he, close to where Princeton is now. The town itself began in 1851 as a roadhouse, the Sixteen-Mile House, and later shipped grain down the river by boat. For nearly 130 years a ferry carried people across the river at Princeton, until it shut down for good in the late 1990s.

places.name: Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge
places.text: The marshes just east of the freeway are the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1937. Fall is the big show. On the refuge's own calendar, waterfowl counts average about 1.5 million in October and 1.8 million in November, when geese arrive by the thousands. The refuge has a visitor center and a 6-mile auto tour.
places.more: The Civilian Conservation Corps built the first wetlands here between 1937 and 1942, on dry, alkaline land between Willows and Maxwell. Before settlers arrived, much of the Sacramento Valley was seasonal wetland and grassland, and less than 10 percent of those wetlands remain. Migrating birds kept coming anyway and ate rice in the fields, so the refuges were created partly to settle that conflict between the birds of the Pacific Flyway and farmers. At dusk in November, flocks still fly off to feed in the rice. More than 250 kinds of birds use the refuge, from snow geese and white pelicans to bald eagles.
places.spot: Look for big white flocks of geese resting on the marsh.

places.name: Mendocino National Forest
places.text: The mountains on the western skyline are the Coast Range, home of the Mendocino National Forest, which has its headquarters in Willows. The forest covers about 913,000 acres in six counties, and it is the only national forest in California without a major paved road entering it.
places.more: President Theodore Roosevelt set the land aside in 1907 as the Stony Creek Forest Reserve. It was renamed the California National Forest in 1908, and in 1932 President Herbert Hoover renamed it again, to Mendocino, to avoid confusion with the name of the state. The forest holds four wilderness areas, the largest of them the Yolla Bolly-Middle Eel. In 2020 the August Complex, which began as 38 separate lightning fires, burned mostly through this forest and grew to more than a million acres, the largest wildfire in California history. Tule elk, once hunted nearly to extinction, were brought back to the Lake Pillsbury basin in the late 1970s.
places.spot: Look for a long wall of mountains along the western horizon.

places.name: Willows, the cattle stop
places.text: Willows takes its name from a shady watering place ringed by willow trees, where cattle drivers traveling through the valley stopped to rest. The post office opened in 1862 as Willow, singular, and did not add the s until 1916. The town has been the seat of Glenn County since the county was created in 1891.
places.more: Willows incorporated in 1886. Fires swept through downtown twice in the 1880s, and each time the town rebuilt, finally replacing its volunteer bucket brigade with a formal fire department in 1887. The Glenn County Courthouse was finished in 1894, and its central dome came off for safety reasons in 1951. The airport opened in 1928 as a training ground for early pilots, and in World War II it hosted practice missions linked to the Doolittle Raiders. In 1979 the state finished building Interstate 5, making Willows a handy stopover between Sacramento and Redding.

places.name: Hugh Glenn, the Wheat King
places.text: Glenn County is named for Hugh Glenn, a doctor who came west in the Gold Rush and became California's Wheat King. His land along the Sacramento River grew to 55,000 acres. At harvest he hired 150 men, and on August 8, 1879, his crews brought in 5,779 bushels of wheat in a single day.
places.more: Glenn trained as a physician in St. Louis and left Missouri for California in 1849 with an ox team and a wagon. He became a cattle rancher, then bought 8,000 acres of Rancho Jacinto and kept adding land until he owned the whole rancho. His ranch had its own blacksmith and machine shops. In 1879 he ran for governor and lost. A horse breaker named Peter French rose to be his foreman, took 1,200 head of cattle to Oregon for him, and later married his daughter. On February 17, 1883, Glenn was shot from ambush on his ranch by his bookkeeper, Huram Miller, several days after Glenn had struck him for his drunken insults.

places.name: Artois, once Germantown
places.text: Artois was called Germantown until 1918. Local belief holds that during World War One, a troop train stopped here for water and the soldiers took offense at the German name. Petitions to change the post office name succeeded, and on May 21, 1918, Germantown became Artois, after the battles fought in that region of France.
places.more: The Germantown post office had opened in 1877. Artois, the old French province behind the new name, is also where people first bored artesian wells. The little town sits on the old U.S. Highway 99W, and Interstate 5 bypasses it just to the west. The rail line through town was once part of Southern Pacific's route up the west side of the valley. On June 1, 2011, a tornado touched down east of Artois, uprooting hundreds of almond trees and damaging farm equipment. About 300 people live here today.

places.name: Prune orchards
places.text: Some of the orchards in the northern Sacramento Valley are prune plums, grown to be dried. Tehama and Glenn are among California's leading prune counties, and California grows more than 90 percent of the nation's prunes and about 40 percent of the world's. Harvest runs from mid-August into early September and usually takes about 30 days.
places.more: California prunes are the Improved French variety, an offshoot of La Petite d'Agen, a plum from southwest France. During the Gold Rush, a Frenchman named Louis Pellier found little gold and turned to growing prunes, grafting the French plum onto wild American plum trees. The fruit's high sugar lets it dry without fermenting around the pit. At harvest, machines grab each trunk and shake the plums onto catching frames, and in the dryers three pounds of fresh fruit become one pound of prunes. A new tree takes four to six years to bear and can yield 150 to 300 pounds of fruit a year. During a labor shortage in 1905, one grower even tried using 500 monkeys to pick the fruit. They picked well, but they ate the crop.

places.name: Orland, Queen Bee Capital
places.text: Orland calls itself the Queen Bee Capital of North America. In 2017 the city council adopted the title because of how many queen bees the town's locally owned commercial apiaries produce. Orland even has a museum about bees, the Honeybee Discovery Center, and it holds a Queen Bee Festival every June.
places.more: The Honeybee Discovery Center says about 80 percent of the queen bees used in the United States are raised in Butte, Glenn, Shasta and Tehama counties. To raise queens, a beekeeper moves larvae less than a day old into special queen cups inside a strong hive that has no queen, and the worker bees feed them royal jelly. After about 10 days the queen cells go to small mating hives. About a week after hatching, each young queen flies out to mate with 10 to 20 male bees. Back home, a queen is usually the mother of most of the bees in her hive, which can hold 60,000 to 80,000 of them.

places.name: Will Green's water notice
places.text: East of Orland, on the Sacramento River, lies Hamilton City. Nearly 4 miles north of town, on December 18, 1883, Will S. Green posted a notice on an oak tree on the river's west bank, claiming 500,000 miner's inches of river water to irrigate the west side of the valley. The spot is now a state historical landmark.
places.more: Green packed a lot into one life after arriving in San Francisco in 1849 and in Colusa County in 1850. He was a ferryboat captain, mail carrier, surveyor, newspaper editor, writer and legislator, and later served as U.S. Surveyor General and as California's State Treasurer. Hamilton City itself began in 1905 with a big sugar beet plant, finished the next year by James Hamilton and the Alta California Sugar Beet Company. The plant, later owned by Holly Sugar, closed in 2006, but its tall silos can still be seen from all over town.

places.name: Stony Creek
places.text: The freeway crosses Stony Creek just north of Orland. The creek was named for the loads of rock and sediment it once washed down from the mountains in floods, and it was once called the Capay River. Today Black Butte Dam, built in 1963 in the foothills to the west, traps most of that sediment.
places.more: Stony Creek runs 73.5 miles and is the second largest stream feeding the Sacramento from the west, after Cottonwood Creek. In 1845 a party led by Peter Lassen quarried grindstones on one of its tributaries, now called Grindstone Creek, and took them down the river to sell at Sutter's Fort and San Francisco. In 1906 Congress authorized the Orland Project to irrigate farms with the creek's water, and the first water arrived in 1910. Without fresh gravel from upstream, the creek below the dam now eats away at its own banks, an effect called hungry water.
places.spot: Look for a gravelly creek bed under the bridge, often dry in summer.

places.name: Paskenta Band of Nomlaki
places.text: Rolling Hills Casino, beside the freeway, belongs to the Paskenta Band of Nomlaki Indians, the Hill Nomlaki people of this part of the valley. In 1959 the federal government terminated the tribe's rancheria and its land was sold. The Paskenta Band kept its identity and culture and won back full tribal status in 1994.
places.more: In 1854 the government set up the Nomi Lackee Indian Reservation in the foothills west of here, a military post that controlled 300 to 2,500 Native people. In 1866 they were moved to Round Valley. The Paskenta Rancheria was created in the early 1900s, and by 1920 it covered 260 acres. After its restoration, the tribe signed a gaming compact with the state in 1999 and opened the casino in 2002. Today the tribe has about 240 members, is headquartered in Corning, and has a rancheria of about 2,000 acres.

places.name: Walnut orchards
places.text: Many of the orchards in Tehama County are English walnuts. In 2024 the county had about 31,000 acres of bearing walnut trees, worth about 95 million dollars, its second most valuable crop after almonds. California grows 99 percent of the commercial walnuts in the United States.
places.more: California walnuts make up about three-quarters of world trade, and about a third of the crop is exported. The most planted variety, the Chandler, was developed at UC Davis and caught on in the 1980s. Walnuts were first grown mainly in Southern California, but by 1910 oranges and lemons were crowding them out of Los Angeles and Orange counties, and orchards spread into central California. Average yields have climbed from about a third of a ton per acre in the 1920s to about 2 tons.

places.name: Lassen's rancho and Stanford's vines
places.text: About 8 miles east, near Vina, lay Rancho Bosquejo, the land grant of Peter Lassen, the Danish blacksmith whose name is on Lassen Peak. In 1848 he led emigrants to his ranch over a new route, the Lassen Cutoff. Signs his agents later put up promised Gold Rush travelers that the diggings were only 110 miles away, but the cutoff proved about 200 miles longer than the main trails.
places.more: Lassen got his grant in 1844 after becoming a Mexican citizen, and in 1845 he laid out a town on Deer Creek called Benton City, but its settlers soon left for the gold fields. In 1881 Leland Stanford bought the land and built the Vina Ranch, with what was then the largest vineyard and winery in the world. The vines made poor wine, so brandy became the main product. After Stanford died, the ranch went to Stanford University, which sold it off piece by piece. Today a Trappist monastery, the Abbey of New Clairvaux, occupies part of the old homestead.

places.name: Corning, olive town
places.text: Corning began in 1882, when the railroad was extended to this point, and it was named for John Corning, a railroad official. Its biggest local industry is growing and preparing table olives. Corning is home to Bell-Carter Foods, maker of Lindsay Olives and the largest table olive processor in the United States.
places.more: Just off the freeway, the Olive Pit started out as a burger and shake stand on a small piece of land that Pete and Ann Craig bought in 1967. They bet that the soon-to-be-finished Interstate 5 would bring travelers, and they stocked a shelf with a few small jars of olives from their family's orchard. Today the Craig family is Corning's largest seller of olives and olive oil. The Corning Olive Festival, held on the second Saturday in October, began in 1946 as a fundraiser for the local Catholic church and is called the longest-running olive festival in the country. In 2024, Tehama County's table olives were worth about 25.6 million dollars, from about 3,900 acres of bearing trees, and oil olives covered about 3,800 acres more.

places.name: Helmick rest area
places.text: These rest areas are named for Lieutenant John C. Helmick, the California Highway Patrol's Red Bluff Area commander. On February 27, 1989, while driving to speak at a Rotary Club luncheon in Oroville, he was killed when his car crashed into a Caltrans truck parked on the shoulder of Highway 99. He was 43.
places.more: Helmick was a 20-year veteran of the Highway Patrol and had led the Red Bluff Area for three years. The rest areas here were first built in 1965. Caltrans completely rebuilt them starting in 2015, and they reopened on May 8, 2017, with LED lights, low-flow plumbing, shade structures and drought-tolerant plants. As a finishing touch, the builders added sundials around each flagpole.

places.name: Thomes Creek
places.text: The freeway crosses Thomes Creek here, named for Robert Thomes, a pioneer who arrived in the 1840s. His name has been misspelled so often that official records list the creek as Thomas Creek, Thoms Creek and Toms Creek. The creek runs about 62 miles from the Coast Range to the Sacramento River, with no permanent dams.
places.more: It is a highly seasonal stream. In summer its wide bed of gravel and boulders is often dry, but on December 22, 1964, during that year's Christmas flood, it carried 37,800 cubic feet of water per second. The creek begins at a small pond called Kingsley Lake, 6,460 feet up in the Mendocino National Forest, and its upper 22 miles are rated very difficult for whitewater kayaking. Steelhead trout and spring-run Chinook salmon still use it.
places.spot: Look for a wide bed of gravel and boulders, often dry in summer.

places.name: Tehama, the first county seat
places.text: About 5 miles east, on the Sacramento River, is the little city of Tehama, home to 435 people in 2020. When Tehama County was formed in 1856, Tehama was its county seat, but a county-wide election moved the seat to Red Bluff the very next year. Because the town floods easily, its houses must sit above flood level, so most have tall stairways to the front door.
places.more: A Nomlaki village of the Wintun people once stood where the town is. The name Tehama is most often said to come from a Wintun word for high water, though other meanings have been suggested. Robert Thomes, who received the Mexican land grant Rancho Saucos in 1844, laid out the town in 1850. For a few years it was the last stop for riverboats, and the river later washed away First Street entirely. Tehama had a freewheeling reputation as the last town in the county to go dry before Prohibition, and its population peaked around 2,000 in the 1890s.

places.name: Gerber, the railroad stop
places.text: East of the freeway, Gerber was platted in 1910 and named for the Gerber family, who owned the town site. From 1916 to 1965 it was a division point on the Southern Pacific Railroad, where steam locomotives took on fuel, got repairs and changed crews. The town also had livestock yards and an icing plant for refrigerator cars.
places.more: Gerber sat two miles north of the junction where the railroad's west valley line to Davis met the east valley line through Chico and Marysville. Once diesel locomotives replaced steam by 1955, the work in Gerber wound down over the next decade. Passenger trains kept stopping until 1972, when Amtrak's Coast Starlight dropped the station. In its early years the town served ranchers and alfalfa growers, and about 1,000 people live there today. Nearby Proberta was laid out in 1886 by Edward Proberta and named for him.

places.name: Red Bluff Diversion Dam
places.text: East of the freeway, the Red Bluff Diversion Dam, a concrete structure nearly 6,000 feet long, crosses the Sacramento River. Finished in 1964, it raised the river to feed the Tehama-Colusa and Corning canals, which water about 150,000 acres of farms. But it also blocked salmon, so since 2013 its gates have been locked open to let the river run free.
places.more: The Sacramento, California's largest river, once had one of the southernmost large runs of Chinook salmon in North America. The count of winter-run Chinook fell from 118,000 in 1969 to a record low of 191 in 1991. Fish ladders and a fish screen did not solve the problem, and in 2009 federal fisheries officials ordered the gates opened year round. A new pumping plant with a fish screen, just upstream, now lifts water into the canals. Locking the gates open was controversial, because it drained Lake Red Bluff, a popular recreation spot. The Tehama-Colusa Canal, the larger of the two canals, runs 110.9 miles down the west side of the valley and was not finished until 1980.

places.name: John Brown's widow
places.text: In the fall of 1864, Mary Brown, widow of the abolitionist John Brown, arrived in Red Bluff with her children, poor and homeless. The town helped her, and a fund headed by Governor Frederick Low raised 450 dollars for a lot and a small house on Main Street. That house is now a California Historical Landmark.
places.more: John Brown had been executed in 1859 after leading a raid on Harpers Ferry, Virginia, meant to start a campaign to free enslaved people. Mary had 13 children of her own and raised 5 stepchildren, and the couple had helped people escape slavery on the Underground Railroad. On the way west, the family was chased by Confederate sympathizers and reached a Union army post in Idaho just three hours before them, and soldiers escorted them 200 miles. In Red Bluff, Mary worked as a nurse and midwife. But she was harassed by pro-slavery people, and in 1870 the family sold the house and moved to Humboldt County.

places.name: Red Bluff, head of navigation
places.text: Red Bluff is named for red bluffs that once stood out along the banks of the Sacramento River, which the freeway crosses twice in town, less than two miles apart. The town grew up at the head of navigation, the farthest point riverboats could reach, and miners landed here bound for the gold fields of Trinity County. It was first called Leodocia, then Covertsburg.
places.more: Red Bluff also marks the northern end of a stretch of farmland that runs almost unbroken to Bakersfield, about 400 miles south. The railroad arrived in 1872, and for a few years the town was the end of the line. In February 1886, thousands of white people in an Anti-Coolie League marched on Chinatown and ordered the Chinese residents to leave within 10 days. The Chinese community refused, called on white merchants who supported them, and stayed. In 2022 the city established a Historic Chinatown District. Every April the town hosts the Red Bluff Round-Up, billed as the largest three-day rodeo in the country, which began unofficially in 1918 when ranch hands held contests on a local ranch. In 2024 it drew 675 competitors and about 35,000 fans.
places.spot: Look for the wide Sacramento River passing under the freeway, twice.

places.name: William B. Ide Adobe
places.text: A mile north of Red Bluff, on the west bank of the Sacramento River, a state historic park honors William Ide, the only president of the California Republic. That republic, born in the Bear Flag Revolt, lasted from June 14 to July 9, 1846, less than a month. Here is the twist: research later showed that Ide never owned or lived in the adobe that bears his name.
places.more: An early Red Bluff settler named A. M. Dibble built the adobe in 1852. About 20 different owners held the property before 1942, and Ide actually owned land farther down the river. The state bought the site in the 1950s, dedicated the park in 1960, and kept Ide's name to honor his part in California history. Today the park has the restored adobe, a recreated 1850s homestead with a blacksmith shop, and a picnic area above the river. In June it hosts the Ide's Ferry Championship Horseshoe Pitchers Contest, and on special days visitors can try Gold Rush card games like faro and monte.
places.wiki: William B. Ide Adobe State Historic Park

places.name: Alvin Coffey's freedom
places.text: Red Bluff was home to Alvin Coffey, born enslaved in Kentucky in 1822. In 1849 his enslaver forced him to California to mine gold, then took him back east and sold him. Coffey returned to the gold fields, mined enough to buy freedom for himself and his family, and in 1857 the family set out for California and settled in Red Bluff.
places.more: On his first trip, his enslaver hired out Coffey's labor as a cobbler, laundryman and miner and kept the money. Coffey later wrote that he thought about escaping, but feared his situation would get worse if he were caught. His new owners agreed to let him buy his freedom for 1,000 dollars, and he worked mines around Shasta and Sutter until he could pay. In Red Bluff the Coffeys farmed, raised turkeys and ran a laundry. In 1887 he joined the Society of California Pioneers, its only Black member, and he is buried at Oak Hill Cemetery in Red Bluff.

places.name: Bend, once Horsethief Bend
places.text: East of the freeway lies the little river community of Bend. It was first called Horsethief Bend, then Sander's Bend, and finally just Bend, after a loop in the Sacramento River nearby. About 600 people live there today.
places.more: Bend had its own post office from 1897 to 1935. Nearby, the Bureau of Land Management's Sacramento River Bend Area protects public land along the river, with habitat for bald eagles, osprey, songbirds, deer and salmon. Boaters launch at Bend Bridge Park. The Jellys Ferry day-use site is a trailhead for the Yana Trail, which fords Inks Creek and can be impassable in wet weather.

places.name: Herbert S. Miles rest area
places.text: These rest areas are named for Herbert S. Miles, a highway engineer who spent 42 years working on California's state highways. As a district engineer, he helped lead the creation of the state's Safety Roadside Rest program. A plaque honoring him stands at the rest area on the east side of the freeway.
places.more: California's modern rest stop system dates to 1963, when a state law directed the state to plan, build and maintain safety roadside rests along its highways. The plan behind that law called for 257 of them. By 1970 all but a handful of today's rest areas had been built. A 1974 plan cut the system to 162, a 1985 plan kept 91 existing ones, and today California has 87. Long before that, in the 1930s, highway crews built roadside fountains and picnic areas, but they were wiped out by highway work after World War II.

places.name: Mount Shasta from afar
places.text: On clear days, the lone peak far off on the northern skyline is Mount Shasta, about 80 miles away. It rises abruptly, towering nearly 9,800 feet above the land around it. On a clear winter day, it can be seen from the floor of the Central Valley as far as 140 miles to the south.
places.more: Shasta is the second-highest peak in the Cascade Range and the fifth-highest in California. Together with its satellite cone, Shastina, it dominates the landscape around it. From the 1820s on, it was a landmark for travelers on the Siskiyou Trail, which followed old Native American footpaths between the Central Valley and the Pacific Northwest, and Interstate 5 is today's version of that trail. The mountain holds religious significance for the Wintu people. The freeway passes close to its base near the town of Weed.
places.spot: Look for a lone white peak far away on the northern skyline.

places.name: Cottonwood Creek
places.text: The freeway crosses Cottonwood Creek here, which forms the line between Tehama and Shasta counties along its whole length. It is the largest undammed tributary of the Sacramento River, which is why it still has runs of Chinook salmon and steelhead. John C. Frémont named it in 1846, describing cottonwoods along its sandy, gravelly bed.
places.more: When Tehama County was created in 1856, the county line was drawn along the creek. In 1851, Wintu leaders signed the Treaty of Cottonwood Creek, giving up most of their land in exchange for a reservation along the Sacramento River, but the state opposed it and it was never ratified. The creek often runs like a large river in winter and spring and shrinks to a trickle by summer. Since the 1940s, the government has proposed big dams on the creek, including one 247 feet tall, but local opposition and concern for salmon stopped them. In 1872, the first train station in Shasta County was built at Cottonwood.
places.spot: Look for a wide creek lined with trees at the Shasta County line.

places.name: Cottonwood, the halfway town
places.text: Cottonwood was a stagecoach town, settled in 1849, and it got its first post office in 1852. It sits halfway between Redding and Red Bluff, 15 miles from each, on both banks of Cottonwood Creek, which gave it its name. About 6,300 people live here now, nearly twice as many as in 2010.
places.more: Cottonwood sits at the southern end of Rancho Buena Ventura, a 26,632-acre Mexican land grant given in 1844 to Pierson B. Reading, a pioneer of 1843. It was the northernmost land grant in California, stretching 19 miles along the west side of the Sacramento River, from Cottonwood Creek to Salt Creek. Reading's adobe home stood about 6 miles east of Cottonwood, near what is now Reading Island Park, and he is buried nearby. In December 2024, a single Mega Millions ticket sold in Cottonwood won a jackpot of 1.22 billion dollars, the fifth biggest in the game's history. Some residents would like Cottonwood to become a city, but the new Sunset Hills and Sun City Tehama neighborhoods lie across the county line, and California's constitution does not allow a city to cross a county line.

places.name: Coleman fish hatchery
places.text: About 7 miles east, on Battle Creek, is Coleman National Fish Hatchery, the largest salmon hatchery in the continental United States. It was built in 1942 to make up for spawning grounds lost when Shasta Dam blocked the river. Its goal is to raise about 12 million fall-run Chinook salmon each year.
places.more: Shasta Dam permanently cut off about half of the key spawning and rearing habitat for Chinook salmon and steelhead in this river system. At Coleman, salmon returning from the ocean swim up Battle Creek and are drawn into the hatchery by the flow of water. Workers collect and fertilize their eggs, and the young fish grow in ponds until they are big enough to head to sea. Besides fall-run fish, Coleman raises late-fall Chinook and steelhead, and a sister hatchery at the base of Shasta Dam raises winter-run salmon. Coleman's fish help support California's commercial and sport fishing.

places.name: Anderson, a railroad town
places.text: Anderson is a railroad town. In 1872, a rancher and hotel keeper named Elias Anderson deeded the Central Pacific Railroad a right of way through his land, and in return the railroad named its depot after him. Today Anderson is a city of about 11,000, and it is the headquarters of Sierra Pacific Industries.
places.more: Sierra Pacific, the second-largest lumber producer in the United States, is the largest private landowner in California, with about 1.7 million acres, twice the area of Yosemite National Park. It runs its own fabrication plant in Anderson to build parts for its sawmills. Elias Anderson bought the American Ranch in 1856 and built the American Ranch Hotel in what became downtown, with the post office inside. The city's Anderson River Park sits on part of his old land.

places.name: Lassen Peak
places.text: On clear days, the big mountain on the eastern skyline is Lassen Peak, about 40 miles away, the southernmost active volcano in the Cascade Range. On May 22, 1915, it blasted a column of ash more than 30,000 feet into the sky. A photograph of that eruption was taken from Red Bluff, about 45 miles from the peak.
places.more: Lassen had been quiet for about 27,000 years when steam explosions began on May 30, 1914, and about 400 eruptions followed through 1921. The big 1915 blast sent a hot avalanche of ash, pumice and rock down the mountain, leaving a 3-square-mile scar now called the Devastated Area. The ash cloud could be seen from Eureka, 150 miles west, and ash was detected as far away as Elko, Nevada. The Mountain Maidu call the peak Kom Yamani, Snow Mountain, and it has the highest known snowfall in California, about 660 inches in an average year. In July 2024, the Park Fire, which began in Chico, burned 429,603 acres of foothills and forest and closed Lassen Volcanic National Park for three weeks, though the flames never entered the park.
places.spot: Look for a big lone mountain on the eastern skyline, often with snow on top.

places.name: Reading's gold on Clear Creek
places.text: Clear Creek joins the Sacramento River just west of the freeway, south of Redding. Five miles up the creek, at a spot called Reading's Bar, Pierson B. Reading and his Native workers found gold in 1848. Both the creek and Reading's Bar are now state historical landmarks.
places.more: Reading's strike came in March 1848, shortly after James Marshall's discovery at Sutter's Mill. Clear Creek is the first major tributary to join the Sacramento below Shasta Dam. It begins in the Trinity Mountains, between Shasta Lake and Trinity Lake, and flows through Whiskeytown Lake before reaching the river. Below Whiskeytown Dam, the Spring Creek Tunnel bypasses the lower creek, carrying water from Whiskeytown Lake straight to Keswick Reservoir as part of the Central Valley Project. The gold discovery site was declared a California Historical Landmark in 1932.

places.name: Redding Rancheria
places.text: West of the freeway, south of Redding, is the Redding Rancheria, a federally recognized tribe of Wintu, Pit River and Yana people. Its 31-acre site was bought by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1922, as a place to camp and live for Native people who had been made landless by settlers.
places.more: The three groups organized as one tribe and were recognized in 1979, and they adopted a constitution in 1989. The tribe is governed by seven councilors elected by its members. It built the Win-River Resort and Casino along Highway 273, near the freeway. The casino's revenue has funded payments to each tribal member.

places.name: The 1846 river massacre
places.text: On April 5, 1846, an armed expedition led by Captain John C. Frémont attacked a large Wintu camp on the banks of the Sacramento River near what is now Redding. The Wintu, most of them women and children, were trapped against the river. Estimates of the dead range from 125 to 900, and no one was ever punished.
places.more: Frémont's party had come up the valley from Peter Lassen's ranch after settlers claimed that Native people were preparing to attack. The camp's men formed a line to shield the women and children, but their arrows could not reach the riflemen. Kit Carson, one of the attackers, later called it a perfect butchery. More massacres of Wintu people followed in the 1850s. Frémont went on to become one of California's first United States senators and, in 1856, a candidate for president. Wintu people live in this region today, including as members of the Redding Rancheria.

places.name: The Carr Fire
places.text: On July 26, 2018, the Carr Fire jumped the Sacramento River into the west side of Redding, and 38,000 people had to evacuate. That evening a fire whirl formed, with winds estimated above 143 miles an hour, as strong as an EF3 tornado, and it rose an estimated 18,000 feet into the sky.
places.more: The fire had started three days earlier near Whiskeytown, west of Redding, when a trailer's tire blew out and its steel rim scraped the pavement, throwing sparks into dry brush. It burned 229,651 acres and destroyed 1,604 buildings, including more than a thousand homes. Eight people died, among them Redding fire inspector Jeremy Stoke, who was killed by the fire whirl. The whirl stayed on the ground for about half an hour, toppling transmission towers and stripping bark from trees. Near Lake Redding Park alone, close to 40 homes burned.

places.name: Redding, once Poverty Flats
places.text: During the Gold Rush, miners found little gold in this ground, and the spot was called Poverty Flats. In 1868 the Central Pacific Railroad's land agent, Benjamin Redding, bought land here for a northern terminus, and the railroad built a town and named it for him. The tracks arrived in 1872.
places.more: In 1874, local legislators renamed the town Reading, to honor the pioneer Pierson B. Reading, whose Mexican land grant it sits on. The name was officially changed back to Redding by 1880. The town grew with nearby copper and iron mining in the early 1900s, and it nearly doubled in size while Shasta Dam was being built. Redding is known for very hot summers: the average July high is near 100 degrees, and on July 6, 2024, Redding hit 119, its all-time record. Yet it can snow too. On December 23, 1968, 16 inches fell in a single day.

places.name: Sundial Bridge
places.text: West of the freeway, the Sundial Bridge, a 700-foot footbridge designed by Santiago Calatrava, crosses the Sacramento River. Its 217-foot mast points due north at a 42-degree angle and casts its shadow on a giant dial. The tip of that shadow moves about a foot a minute, so you can watch the Earth turn.
places.more: The bridge links the two halves of Turtle Bay Exploration Park, 300 acres along the river with a museum, animal exhibits, gardens and playgrounds. The museum has exhibits on the Wintu people, including a full-size shelter. The bridge crosses the river without touching the water, which helps protect the salmon spawning grounds beneath it, and its glass walkway glows aquamarine at night. Redding first budgeted 3 million dollars for a footbridge, and some residents wanted a folksy covered bridge instead. Calatrava's design opened in 2004, three years late, at a cost of 23.5 million dollars, paid for by the McConnell Foundation. The bridge also links to the Sacramento River Trail, which runs about 35 miles to Shasta Dam.

zones.label: Almonds, rice and the Sutter Buttes
zones.text: Almond orchards ring Arbuckle and rice fields spread across the flat valley floor, while the Sutter Buttes rise from the plain to the east.

seasons.winter: Almond pollination season, when the orchards bloom, usually runs from about mid-February to mid-March.
seasons.fall: Ducks and geese arrive in fall, and many rice fields are flooded to give them food and shelter through the winter.

zones.label: Rice fields and wildlife refuges
zones.text: Rice fields spread across the valley here, and the marshes of the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge sit just east of the freeway.

seasons.fall: Ducks reach the Sacramento refuge by the thousands in October, and geese follow in November.
seasons.winter: Waterfowl numbers at the refuge peak in late November and early December.
seasons.spring: In April, shorebirds and songbirds stop at the refuge on their way north.
seasons.summer: Most of the refuge marshes are dry in summer, with only about 15 percent of the wetlands flooded.

zones.label: Willows and Glenn County
zones.text: Willows is home to the headquarters of the Mendocino National Forest, whose Coast Range mountains line the western skyline, and almond orchards grow around Artois.

seasons.summer: Prune harvest starts around mid-August and usually takes about 30 days.
seasons.winter: Tule fog season officially runs from November 1 to March 31.

zones.label: Orland and Corning orchards
zones.text: Orchards of almonds, walnuts, prunes and olives grow around Orland and Corning, and the freeway crosses Stony Creek and Thomes Creek.

seasons.winter: Thomes Creek runs highest in February, on average.
seasons.summer: The wide gravel bed of Thomes Creek is often dry in summer.
seasons.fall: The Corning Olive Festival is held on the second Saturday in October.

zones.label: Tehama County to Red Bluff
zones.text: This is the northern end of a band of farmland that runs almost unbroken to Bakersfield, and on clear days Lassen Peak stands on the eastern skyline.

seasons.spring: The Red Bluff Round-Up rodeo comes to town in late April.
seasons.summer: Red Bluff averages about 100 days a year with highs of 90 degrees or more.

zones.label: Red Bluff rangeland
zones.text: Between Red Bluff and Cottonwood, mildly rugged rangeland separates the valley's crop areas, and on clear days Mount Shasta can be seen on the northern skyline.

seasons.winter: On a clear winter day, Mount Shasta can be seen from the valley floor as far as 140 miles to the south.

zones.label: Cottonwood and Anderson
zones.text: Near the northern tip of the Central Valley, Cottonwood grew up as a stagecoach town and Anderson as a railroad town, with ranch land along Cottonwood Creek.

seasons.winter: Cottonwood Creek often runs like a large river in winter and spring.
seasons.summer: By summer and fall, Cottonwood Creek dwindles to a trickle.

zones.label: Redding
zones.text: Redding sits at the northwestern end of the Central Valley, with mountains on the north, east and west and farmland to the south.

seasons.summer: The average July high in Redding is near 100 degrees.
seasons.winter: Winter brings most of Redding's rain, often with fog, and at times snow.

trivia.q: The Sutter Buttes are the leftovers of what?
trivia.why: They are the eroded lava domes of a volcano that formed about 1.6 million years ago.

trivia.q: Before it was renamed in 1876, what was the town of Williams called?
trivia.why: The Central post office opened in 1874, and the town was renamed for W. H. Williams, who laid out the townsite.

trivia.q: Tule fog, the thick winter fog of the Central Valley, is named for what?
choices: The tule marshes of the valley
trivia.why: It is named after the tule grass wetlands, or tulares, of the Central Valley.

trivia.q: Hugh Glenn, for whom Glenn County is named, was known as the king of which crop?
trivia.why: Glenn owned about 55,000 acres and was nicknamed California's Wheat King.

trivia.q: What was the town of Artois called before 1918?
trivia.why: Germantown was renamed Artois in 1918, during World War One, after a region of France.

trivia.q: Orland calls itself the North American capital of what?
trivia.why: In 2017 Orland declared itself the Queen Bee Capital of North America because of its many queen bee producers.

trivia.q: Besides Mount St. Helens, which volcano in the lower 48 states erupted in the 20th century?
trivia.why: Lassen Peak's eruptions began in 1914, and its biggest blast came on May 22, 1915.

trivia.q: How long did William Ide's California Republic last?
trivia.why: The California Republic lasted from June 14 to July 9, 1846.

trivia.q: What was the river town of Bend first called?
trivia.why: It started as Horsethief Bend, became Sander's Bend, and was finally shortened to Bend.

trivia.q: What makes Cottonwood Creek special among the Sacramento River's tributaries?
choices: It is the largest undammed one
trivia.why: As the largest undammed tributary of the Sacramento, it is known for its Chinook salmon and steelhead runs.

trivia.q: What was Redding called during the Gold Rush?
trivia.why: The ground held so little gold that the spot was called Poverty Flats.

trivia.q: Why doesn't the Sundial Bridge touch the Sacramento River?
choices: To leave room for boat races
trivia.why: Staying out of the water helps protect the salmon spawning grounds beneath the bridge.
